chapters.summary: Council Member Pierina Ana Sanchez convenes the Committee on Housing and Buildings hearing on the administration's approach to construction safety and welcomes the public and the administration, acknowledging Council Members Maloney and Riley.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez opens construction safety oversight hearing

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Sergeant, and good morning.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'm Councilmember Pierina Sanchez, Chair of the Committee on Housing and Buildings.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: On behalf of the committee and the New York City Council, I'd like to welcome all the members of the public and the administration who have joined us this morning.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Before I begin, I just want to acknowledge that we are joined by Council Members Maloney and Riley.

chapters.summary: Sanchez notes New York City has more than 1 million buildings and 40,000 active construction sites, with the Department of Buildings as the chief enforcement agency responsible for keeping tenants, small businesses, and workers safe during construction and renovation.
chapters.title: Sanchez frames scale of NYC building stock and DOB's role

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: New York City is home to more than 1 million buildings and 40,000 active construction sites at any moment.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: The chief agency overseeing this work and the city's construction industry is the Department of Buildings.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: The Department of Buildings plays a critical role in enforcing the rules and regulations that keep the tenants, small businesses, and workers across those 1 million buildings safe.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: When a new building is constructed or an existing building undergoes renovation work, the public should have confidence that this work is being conducted with the utmost integrity and that the working conditions on construction sites are safe for every person involved.

chapters.summary: Sanchez says the city has some of the most rigorous and current construction standards, dating to 2022, but argues those standards only protect the public when the enforcement agency is properly staffed, resourced, and able to ensure developers, contractors, and professionals follow the rules.
chapters.title: Sanchez: strong 2022 codes only work if DOB is resourced

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Importantly, we have some of the most rigorous construction safety standards in the world, and they are up to date.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: The construction codes we have in effect are just from 2022.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: But our standards only protect the public when the enforcement agency is staffed, resourced, and able to ensure that developers, contractors, and professionals are following the rules.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So today, we'll take a closer look at DOB's ongoing efforts to advance construction safety.

chapters.summary: Sanchez cites the Mayor's Management Report showing a 45% decrease in serious or fatal construction injuries, from 557 to 308, but notes falls remain the leading cause and that deaths consistently hover around eight per year, with data trends zigzagging since 2022.
chapters.title: Sanchez reviews injury data, falls, and persistent fatalities

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: We've seen recent encouraging trends in the data.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: In fiscal year 2026, the mayor's management reports noted a 45% decrease in serious or fatal construction injuries, which is down from 557 to 308.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Of those serious injuries, falls remain the leading cause over the past two years.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And while the overall decline can signify real progress, more can be done to identify the persistent causes of both serious injuries and deaths on construction sites.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Deaths which consistently hover around eight per year.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And I have to add that while these numbers seem positive, the trends have also zigzagged up and down since 2022 during my tenure as housing chair, and my usual optimism has a little pause.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: In the same way that New York City seeks to prevent all traffic fatalities through the Vision Zero initiative, we should use a similar data-driven approach to eliminate construction-related deaths entirely.

chapters.summary: Sanchez describes the buckling of two load-bearing columns on the 21st floor of the former Pfizer headquarters in Midtown, questions whether corners were cut, and notes DOB's swift response and subsequent citywide enforcement blitz whose results she wants discussed.
chapters.title: Sanchez raises Pfizer column buckling and citywide enforcement blitz

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Recent high-profile incidents also highlight the need for continued evaluation of our city's construction safety standards.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: The buckling of two load-bearing columns in the 21st floor of the former Pfizer headquarters in Midtown raised significant concerns about whether corners were cut,

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: which unsafe conditions were first identified, what scope of work was approved, how the city can ensure this never happens again.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'm thankful for DOB's swift response to ensure the safety of all of the New Yorkers in the surrounding area, but the incident was serious enough to prompt a citywide enforcement blitz from the department,

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: the results of which we will also be wanting to discuss during today's hearing.

chapters.summary: Sanchez says the committee will receive an implementation update on Local Law 79 of 2024 creating proactive DOB enforcement, and points to a Brooklyn DA indictment of Redcoat Inc. for selling fraudulent site safety training cards to untrained workers.
chapters.title: Sanchez previews Local Law 79 update and Redcoat card indictment

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: On a related note, we will also receive an implementation update for legislation that we championed here in this committee, Local Law 79 of 2024, which created a new requirement for proactive enforcement at Department of Buildings.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Additionally, a recent indictment from the Brooklyn District Attorney's Office raises concerns about the oversight of site safety training credentials.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Last month, the Brooklyn DA charged two individuals and the related company, Redcoat Inc., for creating and selling fraudulent site safety cards to construction workers.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Although the company was authorized to provide site safety trainings, the DA alleged that they sold cards to construction workers who never completed that training.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: We must ensure that all workers are appropriately trained and continue to improve the city's tools for overseeing the companies that fake safety credentials.

chapters.summary: Sanchez repeats her long-standing concerns about DOB staffing, noting the prior administration eliminated roughly a quarter of the budgeted workforce including inspection and safety positions, and that the enforcement division still saw a reduction of 16 positions including seven inspectorial titles.
chapters.title: Sanchez flags persistent DOB staffing and inspectorial cuts

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Excuse me, finally.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I would be remiss if I didn't end with my continued concerns around staffing within the agency.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: In my time as chair of the Committee on Housing and Buildings, I have repeatedly raised concerns about DOB staffing.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Under the prior administration, DOB eliminated roughly a quarter of its budgeted workforce, including positions tied to inspections and safety oversight.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And while the council has fought year over year to recover positions, even in the most recent fiscal year, DOB's enforcement division saw a reduction of 16 positions.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Including seven inspectorial titles.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So I will continue to push for inspectorial and safety agency, excuse me, and safety capacity that the agency needs.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I look forward to hearing more about the administration's approach to construction safety, implementation of recent council legislation, and further opportunities to collaborate toward our shared goal of keeping New Yorkers safe.

chapters.summary: Sanchez thanks her district team, including Deputy Chiefs of Staff Ben Ratner and Kim Castellanos, and the Housing and Buildings Committee staff including Senior Legislative Counsel Austin Malone, Billy Eck, Jose Conde, Derek Spencer, Mohamed Shadid, and others.
chapters.title: Sanchez thanks her team and committee staff

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'd like to take this opportunity to thank my team, Deputy Chiefs of Staff Ben Ratner and

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Kim Castellanos, our District Director Maria Jose Mares, Gerard Fernandez, Soraya Bonilla, Oriana Roa Acevedo, Malia Sardinia, welcome to our new fellow, and Marcus Connor, intern.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'd also like to thank the Housing and Buildings Committee staff,

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Uh,

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Senior Legislative Counsel Austin Malone, Legislative Counsel Billy Eck, Senior Policy Analyst Jose Conde, Senior Policy Analyst Derek Spencer, Data Scientist Mohamed Shadid and Noah Slosberg, and

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Finance Analyst Carla.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Aranjo, and Spencer Kuhn.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And with that, thank you all for being here today.

chapters.summary: Commissioner Ahmed Tigani introduces First Deputy Commissioner Igal Shamash and Deputy Commissioner Guillermo Patino, and describes approximately 1,700 DOB employees overseeing nearly 1.1 million buildings and 40,000 active construction sites, emphasizing the full cycle of inspectors, administrative staff, and attorneys.
chapters.title: Tigani introduces DOB leadership and department overview

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Sanchez and members of the Committee on Housing and Buildings.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: I am Ahmed Tagani, Commissioner of the New York City Department of Buildings.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: I am joined today by Igal Shamash, First Deputy Commissioner, Guillermo Patino, Deputy Commissioner of Policy and Legal Affairs, and several members of the department's leadership team.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Thank you for holding this hearing on the critical issue of construction safety.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: We look forward to discussing the department's efforts to keep New Yorkers safe.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Across New York City's landscape of nearly 1.1 million buildings and 40,000 active construction sites, approximately 1,700 dedicated department employees work every day to support the city's growth and safety.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: I just want to emphasize I mentioned a full number because in addition to our inspectors, it also includes the administrative and clerical staff, the attorneys.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: It is a full, whole cycle of work that happens in order to make this process work effectively.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: As residential and commercial buildings are constructed,

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: or altered, safety is the thread connecting all of our efforts.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: It shapes how our

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Our code development team collaborates with industry to update and refine the construction codes, how our plan examiners evaluate building plans, and how our inspectors assess both active construction sites and existing buildings.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: The regulations we enforce further the agency's mission of ensuring the safe and lawful use of buildings and construction sites across the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: This work ultimately protects all New Yorkers and those who visit and work in our great city, including the construction workers who help build it and maintain it.

chapters.summary: Tigani lays out his testimony topics and details Chapter 33 of the Building Code, which sets core construction and demolition safety requirements including site safety plans, crane rules, controlled demolition, and requirements for licensed construction superintendents on new buildings, full demolitions, and large alterations.
chapters.title: Tigani outlines Chapter 33 regulatory framework and site safety roles

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Today I'm going to address the following broad topics.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: The department's construction safety related regulatory framework, training requirements, education and outreach, enforcement,

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: and technology and innovation.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: The department's regulatory framework relies on the requirements in our codes, particularly Chapter 33 of the New York City Building Code and related department rules.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Chapter 33 sets the city's core safety requirements for construction and demolition work, focusing on protecting the public, workers, and neighboring properties.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: It mandates safe job site conditions, site safety plans for larger projects,

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: stringent requirements for the use of cranes and heavy equipment, procedures for controlled demolition work, and protecting and monitoring of adjacent buildings.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Chapter 33 not only sets requirements for how construction and demolition work is carried out, it also establishes requirements for site safety,

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: professionals at larger jobs.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: For example, it requires a licensed construction superintendent to oversee certain construction and demolition projects,

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: including the construction of new buildings, the full demolition of existing buildings, and large alterations to existing buildings.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: DOB, through rulemaking, has specified the tasks a construction superintendent is expected to perform in fulfilling their code obligations of maintaining a safe site,

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: including a daily inspection of the job site, ensuring compliance with Chapter 33 and with approved construction documents.

chapters.summary: Tigani explains that under Local Law 149 of 2021 DOB has restricted how many job sites a construction superintendent may oversee and will begin enforcing a strict one-job limit with mandatory on-site presence starting early next year.
chapters.title: Tigani details Local Law 149 construction superintendent one-job limit

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Additionally, pursuant to Local Law 149 of 2021, DOB has put restrictions on the number of job sites a construction superintendent can be responsible for and will begin to enforce a strict one-job limit

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: and mandatory on-site presence starting early next year.

chapters.summary: Tigani says DOB uses service notices, construction advisories, building bulletins, the My Building newsletter, social media, quarterly industry meetings, and borough office meetings to keep the industry, building owners, and the public informed of regulatory changes and emerging safety issues.
chapters.title: Tigani describes DOB outreach, notices, and My Building newsletter

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: When DOB makes changes to the codes or our processes, such as changes to the superintendent requirements, it's important to make sure that the industry, building owners, and the public are provided notice.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: To that end, DOB uses service notices, construction advisories, building bulletins, and our My Building newsletter, which I'm going to pitch.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: If you haven't signed up for the My Building newsletter, please go online, add your email.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: We use these tools to keep the construction industry and public informed.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: To provide more detailed guidance to clarify regulatory requirements.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: and alert the industry and the public to emerging safety issues and regulatory changes.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: The department also uses its social media platforms and holds quarterly meetings with various segments of the construction industry and even monthly meetings in our borough office where such issues are discussed.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Ultimately, these proactive outreach efforts ensure that our industry partners, building owners, and the public are well informed and can prepare for changes that will impact them.

chapters.summary: Tigani announces DOB is convening the Mayor's Committee on Construction Safety, a housing plan recommendation, with invitations sent this week and a first meeting expected in November, to examine root causes of injuries, evaluate enforcement tools, and address accountability gaps and extreme weather safety.
chapters.title: Tigani announces Mayor's Committee on Construction Safety

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: The department is always looking for ways to modernize and facilitate safer construction in the city.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: I am proud to say that in partnership with the mayor's office, we are convening the Mayor's Committee on Construction Safety,

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: one of the key recommendations and actions in the housing plan, as part of a broader effort to address injuries and fatalities across New York City's construction industry.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Invitations to the first committee meeting were sent out this week, and the committee is expected to convene in November.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: This effort will bring together labor representatives, workers, industry experts, and senior city officials to examine

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: systematic safety challenges and recommend reforms, which may include legislative reforms that we would work on with the council.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: The committee's mandate includes identifying the root causes of persistent construction injuries and fatalities,

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: evaluating current enforcement tools, and identifying gaps in accountability, particularly where contractors repeatedly violate safe standards.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: safety standards.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: The committee will also assess how emerging technologies can help reduce hazardous tasks and protect workers in extreme weather conditions, which was the focus of the Mayor's Executive Order 17 issued earlier this year.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Through this work, the committee aims to strengthen safety practices while supporting the city's ongoing housing and broader development goals.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Chair Sanchez, we look forward to your participation on the committee.

chapters.summary: Tigani describes the Affordable and Efficient Construction Reform (ACER) Task Force as part of the block-by-block housing plan, working with industry and agency partners to identify code and operational changes that speed construction and lower costs without compromising safety.
chapters.title: Tigani introduces ACER Task Force to streamline construction

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: To further support housing and development, the department recently launched a related effort, the Affordable and Efficient Construction Reform Task Force.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: The ACER Task Force is an initiative aimed at streamlining the development process in New York City and a major component of the administration's block-by-block housing plan.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: The department is working with industry and agency partners to evaluate multiple facets of the agency's regulatory framework to identify areas for improvement, to speed up construction, to make it less expensive to build in the city, but not compromise safety.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: The goal is to develop recommendations for operational changes and modifications to the city's construction codes, a process that's working in parallel to the important work of our code committee process.

chapters.summary: Tigani reports construction injuries fell from 692 in 2023 to 482 in 2024 and 320 in 2025, with 266 so far in 2026, while fatalities were seven in 2023, ten in 2025, and four so far in 2026, stressing that no injury or fatality is acceptable and that training correlates with the decline.
chapters.title: Tigani reports declining construction injuries and fatalities

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: As we shared during the recent hearing on the mayor's housing plan, construction sites are safer than they have been in previous years.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Proactive and complaint-based inspections.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Industry outreach and engagement and mandatory site safety training for workers have contributed to this progress.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: We believe that training is a key component that directly correlates to the downward trend in construction-related injuries and fatalities.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Since calendar year 2023, the number of construction-related injuries on job sites have steadily decreased.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: In calendar year 23, there were 692 reported injuries compared to 482 in calendar year 2024, a 30% decrease.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: In calendar year 2025, there were 320 reported injuries, marking a 34% decrease from the year before.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: And as of September.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: There has been 266 reported injuries thus far for calendar year 2026.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Meanwhile, there were seven construction-related fatalities in calendar year 2023 and calendar year 2024-10.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: There were seven construction-related fatalities in calendar year 2023, 10 in calendar year 2025, and four so far in 2026.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: I want to underscore this.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: There is no such thing as an acceptable injury or a fatality on a construction site.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: We believe with training, education, outreach, those incidents are preventable, and we have to work harder to make it so.

chapters.summary: Tigani says worker falls are the leading cause of injuries and fatalities and are a focus of the SST curriculum, and notes Local Law 10 of 2026 added a mental health module addressing suicide prevention, substance misuse, and workplace stress, shifting the city beyond hard-hat hazards.
chapters.title: Tigani details fall prevention and Local Law 10 mental health module

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: What our data shows is that worker falls are the leading cause of construction-related injuries and fatalities, which makes fall prevention a focus for the department, and that is reflected in the SST training curriculum.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Both the mandated SST training and refresher courses cover fall prevention and a number of other topics.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Further, the City Council, the industry, and DOB collaborated on Local Law 10 of 2026, passed at the end of last year and effective in January of this year, which updated the SST curriculum to include a new

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: mental health module that addresses suicide prevention, substance misuse risks, and the everyday stresses of construction work.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: This reflects a shift in how New York City thinks about construction safety, moving beyond hard hat hazards to the well-being of workers themselves.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: This marks a deliberate evolution on the SST program by acknowledging the human realities of the workforce that builds our city.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: To date, DOB-approved course providers have issued over 396,000 active

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: site safety training cards, nearly 74,000 active supervisor cards, and approximately 114,000 active worker wallet cards.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: DOB continues to conduct outreach regarding the site safety requirements, including through its annual Construction Safety Week event in May.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: an annual construction safety report, and conducting targeted outreach when we identify troubling trends.

chapters.summary: Tigani reports over 396,000 active SST cards, nearly 74,000 supervisor cards, and about 114,000 worker wallet cards, then describes DOB's coordination with DOI and the Brooklyn DA on the Red Code indictment, revoking its provider status and moving to invalidate 2,000 cards, with SBS offering free replacement training.
chapters.title: Tigani cites SST card counts and Red Code fraud enforcement

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: We take site safety training seriously.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: We have taken strong enforcement action against course providers who put the public at risk.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Just last month,

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: DOB coordinated with the Department of Investigations and the Brooklyn District Attorney to investigate Red Code, Inc., leading to an indictment of the company and its principals for selling fraudulent OSHA and

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: safety training cards to workers who never received the required training.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Immediately following the indictment, we revoked their status as a DOB-approved course provider and developed a plan to invalidate all 2,000 active SST cards the company has issued,

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: citing the danger of allowing untrained workers onto job sites and the need to preserve the integrity of the city's construction safety training program.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Simultaneously, the Department of Small Business Services launched a remediation program, urging affected workers to contact the agency and provided free, legitimate replacement SST training through

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: SBS authorized providers so workers could come into compliance and continue to work safely on construction sites.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: These enforcement actions underscore DOB's core responsibility to protect the public by ensuring that every worker on a construction site holds a legitimate, verifiable SST card supported by actual training, not fraud.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: fraudulent credentials that undermine safety.

chapters.summary: Tigani describes how DOB receives complaints via 311, referrals from HPD, FDNY, and OEM, or industry notifications, dispatching inspectors and taking actions such as oath summonses, stop work orders, or vacate orders, including enhanced tools like criminal summonses, affirmative litigation, and disciplinary action against licensees.
chapters.title: Tigani explains DOB complaint sources and enforcement tools

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: As the City Council is aware, the establishment of regulatory requirements and modifications to the applicable codes is only one part of DOB's work.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Ensuring compliance with those requirements is another and includes enforcement of technical and safety standards.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: DOB may receive complaints of potential violating conditions from a number of sources, including 311, a referral from another city agency such as HPD or FDNY or OEM, or a notification from the industry in connection with an incident.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: After notification of an incident or potentially violating condition, DOB inspectors will be dispatched to the building or construction site to inspect.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Where a violating condition is found, appropriate action is taken, which may include issuance of an oath summons, a stop work order, or a vacate order, depending upon the nature of the violating condition.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: In the case of immediately hazardous violations, Class 1,

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: When the owner has failed to certify the correction of violating conditions, the department will re-inspect until all violating conditions are corrected.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: When appropriate, the department utilizes enhanced enforcement tools such as issuing criminal court summonses or initiating affirmative litigation, which requires coordination with the New York City Law Department.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Enforcement actions could also include disciplinary actions against a licensed design professional.

chapters.summary: Tigani describes a January 2026 uncontrolled wall collapse on Walton Avenue in the Bronx where a contractor ignored a full stop work order, demolished out of sequence, and illegally used an excavator; DOB suspended the contractor's registration and issued violations, and he asks the Council to help expand enforcement tools.
chapters.title: Tigani recounts 57 East Burnside Avenue collapse enforcement

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: A response to an incident at 57 East Burnside Avenue in the Bronx is an example of where the department took swift enforcement action in partnership with the chair's office.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: On January 12, 2026, construction crews employed by a general contractor were performing demolition operations at a large single-story building.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: While work was ongoing, a building wall along Walton Avenue experienced an uncontrolled collapse, spilling out onto an adjacent sidewalk shed, sending debris approximately 15 feet onto the roadway.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Fortunately, no one was hurt because of the collapse, which would have resulted in a serious injury.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: DOB's investigation into this incident determined that the contractor ignored a previously issued full stop work order for the site, which legally prevented the demolition from proceeding.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Additionally, the contractor was performing the demolition out of sequence and contrary to the approved engineering plans and was illegally using an excavator to clean up the demolition work.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: DOB took immediate action to suspend the registration of the contractor and issued violations to his employer.

chapters.summary: Tigani says Local Law 79 of 2024 shifted DOB to more proactive enforcement using predictive analytics, with proactive inspections rising from 28% in 2024 to 31% in 2025 and 33% in 2026, run by a 59-person team whose work increases downstream workload for attorneys and clerical staff.
chapters.title: Tigani reports Local Law 79 proactive inspection growth

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Since the City Council passed Local Law 79 of 2024, requiring DOB to create a proactive inspection program, the department has shifted from a primarily complaint-based approach to a more proactive one.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: which strengthens the public safety as it enables us to intervene before major issues arise.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Through the program, DOB uses predictive analytics to focus its resources on the city's most at-risk buildings and on bad actors.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: In calendar year 2024, the department conducted 127,535

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: reactive inspections and 49,431 proactive inspections, with proactive inspections accounting for 28% of the total.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: In calendar year 2025,

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: I meant to say calendar year 2024 before.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: In calendar year 2025, DOB conducted 129,058 reactive inspections and 57,673 proactive inspections,

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: increasing the proactive enforcement share to 31%.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: For calendar year 2026, as of September, the department has conducted 109,793 reactive inspections and 54,226 proactive inspections,

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: further increasing the proactive share to 33%.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: The proactive inspections program is comprised of a team of 59 DOB personnel, which includes inspectorial and administrative staff.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: However, the work of the proactive inspections team and our inspectorial staff in general has a downstream impact on the other areas of the agency when violations are issued.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: That results in an increased workload for other units, such as attorneys who represent the Department of Oaths and the administrative and clerical staff who review and process certificates of correction.

chapters.summary: Tigani outlines technology efforts including DOB Now enhancements, drone inspections, and the Buildings Tech Lab, noting 609 active inspectors with an 8% vacancy rate, and plans to engage Ptolemy for predictive analytics on violation-prone actors and GRIPS for a unified enforcement data dashboard.
chapters.title: Tigani describes DOB Now upgrades and Buildings Tech Lab pilots

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Lastly, I'd like to touch upon technology and innovation and what DOB is doing in that space to improve operations, efficiency, and safety.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Expanding the city's available housing supply remains a priority for this administration.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Further, the department's work as it relates to commercial development directly impacts the creation of jobs and the industries that provide essential services to New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Therefore, it is paramount that we have the technological capacity to support and keep pace with development in the city.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: That includes implementing enhancements to the available modules and functionality in DOB Now, as well as exploring ways technology could facilitate faster building inspections, such as with the use of drones.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: We are continuing our work with the Buildings Tech Lab, a public-private initiative with the Partnership Fund for New York City.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: The Buildings Tech Lab connects technology companies with DOB, subject matter experts, with the goal of identifying, developing, and testing technologies to streamline our processes and improve operations.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Through the Building Tech Lab, DOB is utilizing software to more efficiently route inspectors.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: That means we are able to respond to a larger number of sites.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: That happens in a shorter time frame overall.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: More efficient routing coupled with our high inspectorial staffing level of 609 active inspectors, 14 in the pipeline, and the vacancy rate of 8% overall results in increased productivity and potentially increased safety.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: This fall, the OB plans to engage formally with two firms, Ptolemy and Gripes, to develop the test software to help our enforcement team promote safety on construction sites and in existing buildings.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Ptolemy will focus on using predictive analytics to identify violation-prone actors in the construction and real estate industries and support our enforcement investigations with a particular focus on cases of 10 harassment.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: GRIPS will help bring all agency data into one dashboard to streamline our enforcement operations.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Next year, we plan to engage several more firms through the tech lab to support other aspects of our enforcement mission.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to provide a lot of testimony before you today.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: We welcome any questions you may have, and now I'll take a breath.

utterances.text: It's not just the specific training, and the commissioner mentioned a word just now, culture.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: And that's something that all the outreach, all the training, all the work that we've done with our proactive inspections, we talk about all the time.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: It's changing the culture.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: Safety doesn't mean

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks whether workers fall into unobstructed holes or fail to wear harnesses; Tigani describes a wide range including trip hazards, unorganized sites, improper handling of equipment at heights, and poorly installed temporary stair landings, noting DOB partners with industry groups on tie-off rescue demonstrations and repetition.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash

chapters.summary: Shamash notes worker injuries dropped from 759 in 2018 to 266 so far in 2026; Tigani says over 18 million training hours and over 530,000 active cards resulted from the SST program, and that this platform allowed DOB to quickly add mental health and suicide prevention awareness, with Shamash adding nearly 40 million card taps.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks about the titles, roles, and union status of workers who died in falls; Tigani explains that injuries are self-reported to the agency by owners or competent professionals, making exact roles difficult to determine, but that a variety of trades are affected and that hazards are common across roles.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks about worker roles and union status in fall fatalities

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And do you have any information, you know, regarding, again, focusing, and we will talk about this, I'm sure, in depth in the task force, or you will in the task force, if I'm invited, I will say this,

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: but anything about the titles of folks, the roles of the workers who have fallen to their deaths, any trends there, union, non-union, of the fatalities related to falls?

utterances.text: By local law, if there is an injury on a site, an owner or competent professional on that site must report to the agency.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: So when that report is made by them,

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: through either calling the department or using, we have an online portal that they can use.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: They can self-report that information to us.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: And so we can give you the data of the self-reported style.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: the difficulty would be getting to what exactly is the role.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: But we'll say that it's a variety of different roles on a site that we're seeing different issues come up.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Because very often, whether you're an electrician, a carpenter, a laborer, you're often

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: interacting with any of the things I mentioned earlier that can create a trip hazard, can move you to an elevated position, can have you walking through a site where debris or material is not properly handled and put in the appropriate place.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks how the Affordable and Efficient Code Reform Task Force relates to DOB's regular code revision cycle; Tigani explains the model code program runs every three-plus years with 14 committees and 400 volunteers, and that ACER is a parallel process bringing policy and housing experts together on topics like elevators and alternate materials.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks how ACER Task Force fits the code revision process

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So moving to the A-E-C-R, I know what it stands for.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I don't remember what it stands for.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: But the other task force.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: That is being convened.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you for the invitation.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Received.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: We'll be there.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Oh, Affordable and Efficient Code Reform Task Force.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So can you help us understand how the AECR will...

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Relate to the usual process that DOB undertakes for code revisions?

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: So, you know, since 2008, the model code program, we've continued to work on a regular cycle of every three plus years,

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: refreshing and trying to meet a building code, borrowing from the international code, making sure it meets local needs, local standards.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: The last one, as you mentioned, was 2022.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: That process of over 14 committees, over 400 volunteers, that work is immense.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: I mean, we're pulling from national standards.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: We're pulling from the international building codes.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: We're looking at state and local requirements.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: And from time to time, we have found that to get things done that are equally important but can create a lot of congestion in the code committee work, parallel process, not supplement, parallel process.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: processes could be helpful.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: That is what we did for the existing building code, which we worked on successfully with the council.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: It's actually how we worked on the construction safety laws that we're talking about today, creating a parallel process that got us to the point of success that we're talking about right now.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: So what the Affordable, what ACER, the Affordable and Efficient Code Reform Task Force is doing is looking at a set of issues and questions that have been raised over the years and giving it a

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: more dedicated space to explore and understand whether there are things that we should advance.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: At the very least, have more material discussions.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: And in addition to that, much of our code committee work happens among technical experts with sort of less availability for broader policy and

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: housing-involved industry experts to be in the mix.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Within a dedicated conversation about how they involve in the housing space.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: So we're looking at a broader membership, a broader community that is going to be supplemented by many of the same subject matter experts that are involved in the code committee process.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Coming out of that, and you'll see in the housing plan, we talk about some of the questions and issues that we've heard from community members, both on the industry side and the public side, whether it's looking at

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: These are things that are very, can be very technical.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: And we're bringing the policy experts and the technical individuals together in this supplemental process.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: But the code committee work will continue, and we look forward to working with the council on that.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: All right, so I'm going to turn it to Councilmember Wilson, and then we'll come back.

chapters.summary: Council Member Carl Wilson asks what emerging technologies DOB is considering, especially to shorten the time scaffolding stays up; Tigani describes the innovation board, the T2D2 drone facade inspection pilot with Thornton Tomasetti, and a 2024 report now driving FISP reforms and greater drone and photo imagery use.
chapters.title: Wilson asks about emerging technologies and scaffolding

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Hello, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: I apologize.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: It's late.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: We have dueling committees today.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So I apologize if maybe this was talked about a little bit already, but you mentioned in your testimony about some of the emerging technologies that you're considering to help improve safety standards.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: I'm just curious if you could elaborate a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: I see about the building tech lab, but I'm curious about what other sort of developing technologies you're considering, particularly, you know, scaffolding is the bane of my existence in my...

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: District and many times it's going up for a very long period of time, understandably so for safety reasons, but like what technologies are we looking at to help bring those down faster and not need to have

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: what really appears to be quite a dated

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: safety mechanism up for such long periods of time.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: So I think if you think historically, DOB has a couple of different ways in which we try to engage with new technology ideas.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: First and foremost, we have a innovation board, which we'll call from time to time to answer very specific questions.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: We've used it to look at accessibility opportunities as part of the Where We Live plan, where DOB and HPD partnered to see how we can make our

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: existing building stocks more accessible.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: In 2021, I believe we used the Innovation Board to look at the idea of integrating more technology into facade inspections.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: And there was a program, T2D2, with Thornton Tomasetti, using drone technology, which actually became the bedrock of the later

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: research that we did with Thornton Tomasetti that led to the report in 2024 that now is resulting in both the enforcement laws

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: and policy changes with the council, but also our own efforts to try to amend and create.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: New ways of moving forward with both inspections but work done on facade walls.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: It recommends a greater use of drone technology.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: We're working with a number of universities right now on building out what comes next.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: But if you look at what you

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: We're already seeing we're going to integrate more photo or drone captured imagery for buildings that have to meet their FISP requirements between

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: for buildings that are 40 years or younger and can demonstrate a safe report.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: They'll be able to use technology instead of hands-on inspections for check-ins every three years and not have to do a FIS report until year 12, which is one example that...

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: How we were able to do using the research that we gained.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: I think the other part of it that we want to look at is drone technology overall to see if we can capture data citywide and continue to move that number of 40 years older and older.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: I would say that right now is the first time, the research that we were able to collect, the first time we had database.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Both historically and being able to look forward, facade research and enforcement in the city of New York.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Prior to that, for the 40 years prior to that, we were working off an understanding and individual instances collected over four decades, but not database.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: So now that we have the database, now that we're going to be experimenting with using drone or high-quality photos to examine facades and see how that takes the place of hands-on inspections, we believe we'll be able to do more, and we've signed on some

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: research assistants to be able to help us.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: The other thing I would say is it's not all technology on facades.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Some of it had to do with trying to see if there was a smaller number of drops,

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: if we can extend even the cycle from five to six on older buildings, and then also creating a standardized

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: book or standardized set of rules and approaches that exterior wall examinations can work off.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: We find that there was too much variation in approaches and how people were doing that work.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: That variation translates into higher dollar amounts and different scopes that may cost buildings unnecessarily.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: So we are providing that information, city-sponsored, to create cost savings through that alone.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: So information, guidance, and I think you all will add.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash

chapters.summary: Wilson asks how long clearance to remove scaffolding takes after repairs are submitted and whether prior shed legislation is working; Shamash says owner-design-professional sign-off is immediate for buildings six stories and under, FISP amended reports take two weeks, and Tigani reports about 1,200 sheds removed since January and a shift from one-year to 90-day permits.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: On the, another thing that I, so it's kind of a two-part question.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: The other things that I hear is once building repairs are done and they're ready to bring down the scaffolding, that there's often like a lag time between

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: when their paperwork, everything is submitted for final review and the agency giving clearance to bring it down, even though work has been completed.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So I'm curious what...

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: How long does that usually take if someone has submitted?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And, you know, how long, what's the review period time to bring, to give the clearance to bring the scaffolding down?

utterances.text: And then are there other factors that are contributing to that, like staffing, et cetera?

utterances.text: And then other part is there was a packet of...

utterances.text: Scaffolding legislation and reform that happened in the previous council.

utterances.text: I'm curious if you have any data or metrics to show the effectiveness of that legislation, which was intended to shorten the amount of time that scaffoldings are up.

utterances.text: Answer the first question first.

utterances.text: Depending on the height of the building, so if the building is six stories and less, if the job application for the repairs has been signed off by the owner's registered design professional,

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: that sidewalk shed can be removed as soon as that sign-off occurs.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: And again, that is wholly with the owner's registered design professional.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: If that building is within FISP or Local Law 11, so over six stories in height,

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: our turnaround time for those amended reports, and those amended reports tell us when an unsafe building becomes safe, is two weeks.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: That includes an inspection and a thorough review of the plans and the report that has come in.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: If the building is 15 stories and up, it's site safety.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: It's a major building with regards to facades repair.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: So that is a FISP review from the compliance side, but it's also a full inspection of site safety that occurs as well.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: But our time frame for that is also within two weeks.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: I think speaking to the council legislation, we're continuing to implement new parts of it.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: We just had an announcement recently about movement on rules that we're working to continue to effectuate the goals of that.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: I would say we were able to announce that approximately 1,200 sheds have been down since January, a decrease of more than 15% in 10 months.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: One of the major things I want to highlight is that we have moved from a one-year permit on a shed to 90 days.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: The other linkage is that previously a shed renewal permit would come with just the request of moving the shed forward.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: We are now linking the responsibility of that shed with an explanation of what the owner is doing to alleviate the problem that brought.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: And so there's always going to be a mix of different sheds in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: In fact, it's important that we continue to have pedestrian protection, but we're doing more things to say that this should only be up for as long as it has to be up, and you have to tell us why it's going up.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And are you finding with the 90-day permit that folks are asking for extensions, or is that 90-day period?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: sufficient?

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: I think it's a little bit early in order to make enough of a sample pool to tell you where people are landing with it, but I do think that we still have owners who are

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: working to get the financial wherewithal to make the repairs or working on availability on labor and contracts with the right contractors to do the work.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: And so we're looking at both the outside factors and our own processing time to see how this is impacting the market.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: I'll just add one other thing.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: As of this morning, and the department has a map of all the sidewalk sheds in the city that totals the numbers.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: As of this morning, that number was 6,861.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: At the beginning of this year, I believe we were, as the commissioner mentioned, over 8,000.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: But again, that is a pretty significant drop in 10 months.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: But again, and I was joking a little bit about checking out the sheds in front of 280.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: Once the sidewalk sheds...

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: and the new designs come out and folks start using those new designs, the experience of somebody walking down the block changes significantly.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: And that's the real goal here is to change how the interaction between pedestrians and overhead protection in the city is really felt by the public, right?

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: But one of the recent local laws was to increase the height of the sidewalk shed to allow more light in.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: So you'll see that with the new designs.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: And specifically in front of 280, we have an angled design that lets light in.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: That still does its job, right, making sure that the public is protected.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: But that look and feel is very, very different with the new sidewalk shed designs.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: And then the last thing that is coming into implementation, I believe, in January next year is the civil penalties that we have associated with leaving sidewalk sheds up for over 180 days.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: And that concludes the entire package of local laws.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: And those are the big sticks that we have coming down the pipe.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: So it's the reduction in permit duration.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: It's the reporting every time they renew a permit.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: And then if the owner, very specifically the building owner, doesn't make progress towards affecting those repairs, that's when those civil penalties will be in.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm taking up a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So you already gave me some extra time.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.title: Sanchez asks about after-hours variances and construction volume

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks what punishment applies when contractors work without an after-hours variance, citing videos of work before 5 a.m. and after 9 p.m. at 2501 86th Street and workers without helmets; Tigani says DOB needs an inspector to witness and attest to violations and offers to coordinate scheduled inspections with her office to capture repeated off-hours activity.
chapters.title: Zhuang presses on enforcement of unpermitted after-hours work

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And Commissioner, I have a question.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So after our variance, some of you guys issued the variance.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: If you guys did not issue the variance, they're still doing the work.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Is there any punishment?

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Yes, if we're able to capture a contractor doing work outside of their allowed hours, then there are violations and other follow-up actions we could take as an agency.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So you mean catch their activity there, you guys have an inspector come during that time?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: But the community have recordings saying during this time they have a 24-hour camera there.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: They start work before 5 o'clock in the morning and then still doing the work 9 o'clock at night.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: This happened in my district in 2024.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Also recently, also this year, we called DOB, called 311.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: When 311, DOB come, it's only during work hours.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So during not working hour, what's the plan?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: punishment and how the community reached to DOB?

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: So I can't speak to what the action of someone putting a camera on another person's property, but I can say that when we do get information about after work,

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: after work hours, we try to work with the community to triangulate and schedule inspections if we can and be able to go and capture that action if it's happening during an hour that makes sense for that violation.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Additionally, we work with your office, we work with other community groups, but we do need to have an inspector who is viewing the action and can attest to it to write the violation.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, because I actually personally sent to city administration some videos after hours that the same developer sent to on 2501 86th Street.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: They are coming on Palm Sunday night around 9 o'clock doing the work.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And they also come Sunday doing the work.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And they also come before 6 o'clock in the morning doing the work.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: It's all captured by community, and it's public information.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Everyone knows that.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: You can find at least 10, 20 people testify that.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And also for the...

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: the worker safety.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: When the community worker going to do the construction doesn't wear helmets, who they should report to?

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: They should absolutely call 3-in-1 if they see any dangerous condition so that we can send one of the specialized units to go and inspect and see if something is not being done appropriately.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: And as far as, just to go back to the after-hour variance question, I think our most successful collaborations on going after that is when we work with you or a community member and try to triangle if Sundays are typically where you're seeing the infraction happen.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: If it's Tuesday, Wednesdays, and Thursdays before 7 a.m., we can absolutely plan with our resources in advance to have someone there to capture that.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Because those people, they are playing games with the community.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: They don't respect the community at all.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: They can come in the middle of the night, start the work, and then they can come very late in the evening time, start the work.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We called many times, but...

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We have videos, we have pictures, and the people don't wear helmets.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I just checked my phone in May, just a few days ago, October.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Some people come to 2501 86th Street, they don't wear helmets at all.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: They're going to construction sites.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And I think the

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: The community already reported 311.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Nothing was done there.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: I mean, we have done, as you know, and the community knows, we have done many inspections of the site of 2501.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: That said, our obligation is to respond to all that 311 complaints that come forward.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: So there's no limitation on how often we're going to be responsive and continue to evaluate things.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: If there are particular...

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Time slots or moments where you feel like this is repetitive action.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Right after this hearing, we can coordinate with your office and make sure that we're positioning our resources to be there where it's most actively happening.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: We want to be helpful in capturing activity that shouldn't be happening and issue the violations if appropriate.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Can we just send you pictures and tell you?

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Again, we need to have an inspector who can evaluate that.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Everyone deserves due process in this issue, and so we have to make sure that we're respecting each right as well.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member Joanne.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Council Member Wilson, with a follow-up.

chapters.summary: Wilson asks whether DOB can address property access disputes that keep scaffolding up through arbitration or legislation; Tigani says such disputes are largely governed by state law Section 881 in civil court, and that DOB has clarified netting alternatives and will finalize a netting rule later this year, with arbitration questions remaining at the state level.
chapters.title: Wilson asks about access agreements and arbitration for scaffolding

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you again.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Another question about scaffolding.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm obsessed with scaffolding.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Scaffolding seems to be the topic du jour.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Another reason that I've heard, and I can think of a few specific examples of prolonged erection of scaffolding has to do with disputes over access agreements between properties.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Are there, you know,

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Are there ways that the department is thinking about some procedural or legislative or some kind of change that

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: through something like arbitration, that when there are disputes between properties that we're trying to avoid going to drawn-out legal battles that result with

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: maybe work being completed or not starting yet and keeping the scaffolding up for a sustained period of time that it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Need to be.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: So there is a section of state law 881 and most of these conversations are governed in civil in state civil court where

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: where there were recently in the last couple of years some changes to try to alleviate pressure and move these further along.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: We have heard other suggestions about this but it largely is outside of the OB code lives in civil litigation and largely at the state legislative level.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: The other thing that we did as part of the Shed reform work is also clarify different ways that people can use netting as a way of still meeting their pedestrian protection requirements

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: that may not include staging structural elements on an adjacent property.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: So it's very often given how congested and tight the city is that access is needed, but we are trying to see if there are other netting, other high grade.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: tight netting that can be used to be used in place of sheds, not only to start the work, but keep the work going and complete it.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: So between that and I think that the arbitration or actions at the state level that

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: We're still open to hearing ideas of how the agency can play a productive role.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: There's nothing for the new.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: That netting rule is something that we're working on toward the end of this year.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: And we've already, in the most recent years, put out clarifications on related questions.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So you think legislative changes specifically around arbitration would have to be legislated at the state level?

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: I think most recent discussions have been state-level conversations about Section 881.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: But when it comes to providing information about what's necessary, for instance, we work on a site safety plan that is required and necessary.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: We make sure that's available to the owner and the people doing the work so that when they have those conversations with the adjacent neighbor, they can have substantive conversations and hopefully resolve those discussions more quickly.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Well, I just hope that as we're measuring these new policy changes and we can have an open dialogue about reports about how these,

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: how it's working for the scaffolding timelines.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And I hope you can keep this committee informed about how you're tracking and, you know, what's working and not working.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: All right, thank you so much, Councilmember Wilson.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks what types of incidents caused the eight FY2026 fatalities and how many occurred at sites requiring a site safety manager or construction superintendent; Shamash says five were falls, one was excavation soil work, one was burn inhalation, and one was struck-by, and that only two of the eight sites required a construction super.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks about incident types in FY2026 fatalities

utterances.text: So now I want to move to some questions that I believe were provided to you all beforehand, so they're more numbers and processes kind of questions so that we can all be on the same page.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Moving back to construction-related injuries and fatalities, the MMR reports that construction-related injuries and fatalities, excuse me, injuries fell 12% in FY 2026 from 263

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: to 320, while fatalities stayed at 8.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And I want to correct myself.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez

utterances.text: Five of those, eight were related to worker falls.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks for clarification of the excavation and soil-related fatality; Shamash explains it typically occurs early in a project when digging for a basement or installing a foundation, related to support of excavation or underpinning work.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks what excavation and soil-related fatality means

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And can you help us understand excavation and soil related?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: So that is typically early on in a project when they are looking to install a basement in a cellar building.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: They have to dig down to install foundation or supportive excavation work.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: So that is typically related to what we call SOE or underpinning work.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: To answer your second question, two of those eight locations, 174 Jefferson Street and 3728 Crescent Street,

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: the first one in Brooklyn, the second one in Queens, two of those required a construction super.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: And then to answer your last question, for this fiscal year, July 1st, 2026 to today, we have had only one construction-related fatality.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: That was at 1748 Tudor Road.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: That was a one-family home, no construction super required on that job.
