chapters.title: Sanchez asks how many fatal sites had prior violations or stop work orders

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So of the eight that occurred in fiscal year 2026, only two required a construction superintendent, you're saying.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So six did not.

utterances.text: It doesn't necessarily mean smaller sites.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash

utterances.text: So it could be a larger construction site that is doing a small alteration.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: It doesn't necessarily mean a smaller site.

utterances.text: We'll have to get back to you on the violations.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: I don't have that data right here.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks how many sites the citywide fall protection campaign inspected and how many violations and stop work orders resulted; Tigani says inspectors found hazardous conditions endangering workers at 50 locations, resulting in stop work orders, using the department's dedicated sweep team.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks about 2025 fall protection enforcement campaign

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: DOB data shows that worker falls caused 163 of the 320 construction injuries and six of the 10 fatalities in 2025.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Department of Buildings launched a citywide enforcement and education campaign in response, as you mentioned in your testimony, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: How many sites did the campaign inspect?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: How many violations and stop work orders were issued for fall protection during the campaign?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Were the inspections proactive?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And how were those inspections different from what DOB normally does?

utterances.text: So I can tell you right now that at the end of last year, during the sweep, our inspectors found hazardous conditions endangering workers at 50 separate locations, resulting in stop work orders for these sites.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: And like I said before, we have a dedicated team for sweeps, so this is a typical tool that we would use whenever we see an issue crop up that we need to handle.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks how many sweeps the campaign conducted in total; Tigani says DOB spent the month of December going through all five boroughs to check code compliance and engage workers, and Shamash adds that DOB also handed out flyers and spoke with workers and general contractors as part inspection and part education.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks how many sweeps the fall campaign conducted

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And so how many sweeps were conducted in total as a result of that campaign?

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: I think it's in the month of December, we sort of spent that month going through all five boroughs to check for code compliance and engage directly with workers on best practices.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: I would just add as part of that sweep, we also created some educational materials that we, and so it wasn't just

utterances.text: the inspections that we did as part of that sweep, but we also handed out flyers at those specific job sites.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: We spoke with workers.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: We spoke with the general contractors themselves.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez notes the "other" incident category accounted for 102 of 320 injuries and three of ten fatalities in 2025 and asks what it includes; Shamash says it covers burns, hazardous fumes, electrocutions, and struck-by incidents, among many others, and is a category DOB constantly examines.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks what incidents fall in the "other" category

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: My next question is about the other, the category of fatalities and injuries, the incident type called other.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: In 2025, the other category accounted for 102 of the 320 injuries and three of the 10 fatalities.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: The second largest category after worker falls, I think you already gave me.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: For the fatalities, but for the injuries, can you give us an understanding of what kind of incidents DOB places in the other category?

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: And yes, and

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: a little specific, but the other category has a lot into it.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: For example, burns, hazardous fumes, electrocutions, struck by.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: It is a category that we constantly look at because it is a multitude of things that go into that other category, and we realize it's a large category,

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: but it is something that has a variety of elements to it.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks whether DOB plans to break the large "other" category into subcategories; Shamash says that as DOB shifts to DOB Now Inspections Plus in phased rollout through this year and next, the department will do exactly that.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks whether DOB will split the "other" category

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Do you have any plans to break that category up into different subcategories?

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: Yeah, as we're shifting our system from our current system into DOB Now Inspections Plus,

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: which hopeful happening towards the end of this year in phases and into next year, we will be doing exactly that.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks what criteria DOB uses to classify sites as union or non-union, who reports it, and whether DOB verifies; Tigani says reporting is self-identification without third-party verification under Local Law 78 of 2017, and that the former Pfizer headquarters was an open or mixed shop with both union and non-union trades.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks how DOB classifies union vs non-union sites

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: DOB's construction incident reporting classifies sites as union or non-union.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Many sites, however, employ both union and non-union workers through different contractors and subcontractors, such as in the Pfizer partial collapse.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: What criteria does DOB use to classify a site as union or non-union?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Is the classification...

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: based on the general contractor, the share of union workers on the site, or the trade involved in the incident?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Who reports the site's union status to DOB?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Does DOB verify?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And finally, would DOB classify the former Pfizer headquarters conversion in Midtown as a union or non-union site?

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: So as a result of Local Law 78 of 2017, which was worked on by both the agency and administration and the council,

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: a number of steps were created to make sure that we were capturing details of an incident.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: I mentioned earlier that...

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: When there is an incident, people are required to report within three business days, and through that portal or that call, it is a self-identification, self-verification.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: We do not do a third-party check on that verification, but that information is also available on our website, so we make it available to the public.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: And there is a column specifically asking to verify.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: non-union versus union.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: As far as the Pfizer building, based on what we know, we understand it was an open shop or mixed shop site with both non-union and union trades that worked on that site.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So the only time that DOB learns whether a site is union or non-union is when there is an incident that is reported that answers the question.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Again, our priority is regardless of affiliation, we...

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: focus on the worker, the incident, the accident, and how to prevent it in the future.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks what enforcement followed the July 2026 stop work order at 222 Broadway after cracked beams were repaired without notice; Shamash says DOB issued numerous violations including failure to notify to the site safety manager, construction super, general contractor, and special inspection agency, plus a commissioner's order for monitoring, weekly reports, and peer review, and Tigani says the stop work order was later lifted.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks about 222 Broadway stop work order

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So next up, on July 23, 2026, the department issued a

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: full stop work order at 222 Broadway after learning that two cracked beams on the 32nd floor had been repaired in March 2026 without notice to the department.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: What enforcement action has DOB taken for this failure to notify, and is the stop work order still in place?

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: At 222 Broadway, we issued numerous violations to numerous entities and, as you mentioned, a full stop work order to the site.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: We issued a fail to notify.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: To all the site safety professionals, the site safety manager, the construction super, the general contractor, and the special inspection agency, in addition to numerous other violations.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: We also issued...

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: commissioners'order to the developer and the general contractor to implement an immediate monitoring protocol,

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: weekly engineering reports to be submitted to the Department of Buildings, and then a peer review requirement on the structural design and the addition.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: And the stop work order, after the peer review was completed and all the necessary reports submitted to the department, we lifted the stop work order.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks whether DOB returns to confirm corrective work after a stop work order; Tigani explains owners must submit means-and-methods analysis and a corrective action plan that DOB reviews before lifting the order, and Shamash adds the department does not blindly accept remediation plans and re-inspects immediately hazardous violations through its hazardous re-inspection program.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks how DOB verifies stop work order corrections

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So I thought I had it somewhere, but I'm going to just ask it off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: For these full stop work orders, stop work orders, I'm understanding from your opening testimony, Commissioner, and from your answer just now, Deputy Commissioner, that the agency essentially keeps going back to see if

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: dangerous conditions have been corrected.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: I would just amend this.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: So if there is a partial stop work order or a full stop work order, the contractor, responsible person, the owner, knows that they have a responsibility to provide us with a means and method analysis and a corrective action strategy.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Related to the issue that brought on that violation and action.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Once that is submitted to the department and reviewed, and if an inspection is required, an inspection, then we'll take the steps to lift that partial or full stop work order.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: But there is a process that's involved, and it's contingent on the owner to demonstrate that they understand what was wrong, they corrected what was wrong, and they'll allow them to move forward.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So they submit to you means and methods.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: They submit to you what their corrective action plan is, and then you accept that in every case you go back and check that they're doing the work correctly?

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: I'll just add one other statement.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: If we don't hear back and it is an immediately hazardous violation, we will re-inspect as part of our hazardous re-inspection program.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: So if we do not hear back from them, we will re-inspect.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: To answer your question just now, no, we don't just blindly accept their remediation plan.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: We have a whole team at the department that reviews any kind of documentation related to stop work orders.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: You know, depending on what the remedy is in the violations, it could be a litany of things that need to get submitted to us.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: And then we go and review the corrective action that has taken place on site to make sure it has been implemented and an inspector will go out and confirm that.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks how DOB enforces SST card requirements following the Red Code indictment; Tigani says compliance and risk assessment oversees 126 registered course providers, conducted 154 audits in FY2026 resulting in 17 denials, and Red Code was among those denied, with cases referred to DAs and DOI through audits and community tips.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks how DOB enforces SST card requirements

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So you talked in your testimony, I talked in my opening about, what is it?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I don't have the name here.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Red code?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Red card?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Red code?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: September 2026, the Brooklyn DA, you all and the Department of Investigation worked together to bring an indictment on Brooklyn-based construction training company for fraudulent SST cards.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So can you share...

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Broadly how do you be enforces SST card requirements?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Are you going on site?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Are you spot checking proactively?

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: So our SST card work sits a lot, most of it sits with our compliance and risk assessment work.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: I think right now we're at 126 confirmed, sorry,

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: So we're at 126 SST course providers registered with Department of Buildings.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: In fiscal year 26, we conducted 154 audits, resulting in 17 denials.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: As of July 1st, 2025, was given us more oversight years that course providers must register to become course providers.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: And while there's been 17 denials, others have been approved.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: I'll note that Red Code was one of the 17 that were denied, both in this case with Red Code, another case, Valor, which was an even more egregious case

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: that we worked on with the Manhattan DA's office.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Often we're, you know, through our audits or tips that we get from the community, we're putting in information and we're making these referrals to our partners in the DA office or DOI or both since they have prosecutorial.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Powers to be able to take action.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks whether inspectors check each worker for an SST card on job sites; Tigani describes card taps and on-site worker conversations, and Shamash details how investigators audit course providers by sitting in on classes and checking attendance, and confirm card compliance with construction supers and spot checks using QR codes.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks whether inspectors check each worker's SST card

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: What about on job sites?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Are inspectors checking each worker for an SST card?

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: There are two elements here.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: One, the taps are one way of demonstrating that there's a

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: There's an exterior barrier that's making sure people are tapping.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: But then if we are on a construction site, we may talk to workers to make sure that people are doing what they're doing.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: supposed to and have the cards that they're supposed to.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: I'll just add with regards to the course providers, we have a team of investigators that audit those course providers.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: So they will check that the curriculum matches what's required.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: We will ensure that we are getting their course catalogs and time on those courses.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: We will pretend to be workers and sit in on those classes and make sure that the entire training is happening.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: We will check attendance records for those courses.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: We have a very in-depth check that we do on these course providers.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: With regards to the site safety card requirements, we do confirm with the construction supers, site safety coordinators, managers, and check the logs that all the workers on site

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: have the necessary SST requirements, and then we'll do a spot check on site with specific cards.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: Each card has a QR code that we can check to ensure that it is a valid card.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks what happens to the money Red Code took from workers who paid for fraudulent cards; Tigani says the Manhattan DA may pursue restitution while DOB and Small Business Services run a 90-day free remediation training program, noting many affected workers are Bengali speakers and DOB is doing outreach through Bengali media.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks what happens to money workers paid for fraudulent cards

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Red Code, what happens to the million dollars that they stole from the workers who paid for the fraudulent cards?

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: So I think the Manhattan DA can look at a number of different enforcement acts.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: that they pursue as part of their prosecution.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: In the interim, we, you know, maybe workers who didn't realize they were part of a scheme.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: And so that's why, in addition to the enforcement action, there is also the remediation work that we do with small business services, which has had a history of providing accessible

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: and free training so that those workers, through the transition period of 90 days, can get the training they need to get back on sites.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: I think it's also important to note that these are immigrant communities that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: So we've put equal strength in doing the education and awareness out education in English, but many members of this particular, that use this particular training

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: facility spoke Bengali.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: And so we've been working extensively to connect with Bengali news outlets, doing videos in Bengali to get them aware that they need to come in, get retrained so that they can continue doing their work.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks whether SST courses are available in multiple languages and whether they are generally free; Tigani says many providers offer multiple languages and DOB seeks more, and that while some courses are paid, SBS has long provided free programs often in partnership with worker rights and immigrant-serving organizations.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks about course languages and whether training is free

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And the classes are available in multiple languages?

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: There are many providers who provide multiple languages, and we're always looking for more course providers to meet other edges of the space.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And are the courses generally free, or this is just a case for the red code?

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: They're both.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: So we have courses that are paid for courses, and then SBS, since the beginning,

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: 196 has worked to provide free programs.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: And I think a lot of them are also there through collaboration with worker rights organizations and organizations that work with immigrant communities that are mission driven, who understand that the price point can be hard.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Safety logs.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I've been waiting all hearing to ask you about these.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Everyone has.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: This is why we're all here.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Very, very exciting.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks how and when DOB checks site safety logs and whether they are submitted; Tigani says site safety logs are checked at every inspection, whether routine, unannounced, or incident-related, and that 32,472 sites got a log review in FY2026, resulting in 260 oath summonses for missing, incomplete, or falsified logs.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks how DOB reviews site safety logs

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So DOB requires site safety managers, coordinators, and construction superintendents to keep safety logs.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: How does DOB check whether site safety logs are kept and if reports are accurate?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: When does DOB review these logs?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Is it during a routine inspection, an announced visit, or only after an incident?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Do they submit them?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And I'll stop there because this is like a seven-part question.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: So the department does require these documents as necessary to verify compliance.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: We check for site safety logs at every inspection.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: It's done during the routine, the unannounced, or...

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: The incident inspection incidents, I think you asked us to look at fiscal year 2026.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: All site inspections included a site safety log review.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Total sites inspected, which included a site safety log review, is 32,472.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: And if I can go forward, because I'm sure you'll also want to know about missing and complete or falsified logs.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: That we issued.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: 260 oath summonses in fiscal year 2026 for missing and complete or falsified logs.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: How do you know that they're falsified?

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks how DOB determines logs are falsified; Shamash says inspectors review not just the current day's log but the history to spot discrepancies, cross-check the average number of workers on site against the logs, and perform SST spot checks, noting construction safety inspections are thorough rather than quick.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks how DOB detects falsified safety logs

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Are you checking for cadence of entries into the log?

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: I mean, that's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: You go out and speak more.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: So they'll review not just the logs for that day, but they'll review the history of the logs and ensure that there isn't any discrepancies in those logs.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: And that's just part of the inspection and the inspection checklist that our amazing construction inspectors, walking the sites,

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: they can take a look at the average number of folks that they're seeing on site, making sure that matches the logs.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: And as I said, they'll do spot checks on the SSD requirements.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: So construction safety inspections are not quick inspections.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: And our inspectors are very thorough when they do those inspections.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks whether site safety logs are marble notebooks or electronic; Tigani cites a 2024 building bulletin allowing digital formats and says many sites have moved to digital, and Shamash explains digital records speed reviews and require on-site tablets for inspectors to check worker names and site safety plans.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks whether safety logs are paper or electronic

utterances.text: Are these electronic logs?

utterances.text: There is a, there is, I kind of wish they were, I mean, I'm nostalgic for marble.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: There's actually a building bulletin that we issued out in 2024 that talks about the format, allows for a digital format.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: We require these documents, and we're seeing a lot of...

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: A lot of sites moved to digital, quite frankly.

utterances.text: It would be...

utterances.text: But the bulletin that allowed for transition from paper to digital not only helps the industry, but it helps us as well.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash

utterances.text: I've never said that in an upbeat tone in my life.

utterances.text: It's hitting you well.

chapters.summary: Sanchez describes the 2018 injury at 578 Cozine Avenue where an oath hearing officer dismissed DOB summonses for lack of jurisdiction because DEP had authority, and asks how common such jurisdictional changes are; Shamash explains the DEP-DOB abatement workflow and joint worker safety plan review, and Tigani notes OSHA's ongoing federal oversight role.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks about jurisdiction gaps raised by 578 Cozine Avenue

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So turning to the unfortunate tragedy at 578 Cozine Avenue in Brooklyn, where a...

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Worker was seriously injured in 2018.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: This was a situation where DOB cited the property owner and the asbestos contractor working at the site for failing to save

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: the workers, an oath hearing officer then dismissed the summons because DOB didn't have jurisdiction over the site when the incident happened, DEP had jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So just looking at 578 Cozine Avenue as an example, are these sort of changes in jurisdiction on job sites?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: common?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Have you been able to identify gaps in enforcement?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Because I understand, we understand that at 578 Cozine Avenue, there was no agency that held that work site accountable because of the jurisdictional issues between the agencies.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: We can look into the specifics related to this address.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: The normal flow between DEP and DOB is the abatement work needs to be permitted first and completed, and then the ACP-5 or the ACP-2021 submitted to the department

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: before we issue a permit for the work associated.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: With our work.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: So that is generally the time, the flow of how the work occurs.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: There is an overlap between the work that DEP does and DOB does on certain jobs and depending on

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: On those jobs, what's known as an A-True filing or a worker safety plan has to be submitted, and both DEP and DOB review those worker safety plans

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: specifically associated for when abatement work needs to happen.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: The only thing I'll add here is that in all cases,

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Because of the federal role here, OSHA continues to have oversight, and we work closely with OSHA either in information capacity, coordination capacity, so

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: where OSHA is involved, and we can...

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: of assistance when these incidents happen.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: We do that as well.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Yeah.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks whether DOB meets monthly with OSHA and NYCOSH; Tigani says OSHA meetings are monthly but NYCOSH is not met with monthly though there is a line of communication, and Shamash describes monthly OSHA meetings covering incidents, joint investigations, and how OSHA relies on DOB's fatality investigative reports.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks about OSHA and NYCOSH coordination

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And you're meeting with both Osha and Naikash on a monthly basis?

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: I don't believe it's a monthly.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Osha is monthly, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Osha is monthly.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: I mean, I've recently, we've recently talked to Charlene and Naikosh.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: I think we're trying to involve them, particularly as we approach this committee and think about what more we can be doing.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: We certainly are talking to them earlier in the year as they put together their stats and numbers and put their findings.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: So there is a line of communication, but we're not meeting with Naikosh monthly.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: With regards to OSHA and our monthly meetings, that is headed up by Jill's team, our assistant commissioner for construction safety engineering.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: Our monthly meetings, we go over all necessary incidents that happen over that month.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: It might be worker injury or fatality.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: We go over the investigations that we are doing, that they are doing, the enforcement actions, and then the investigations.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: A lot of times the investigations and the interviews of the workers happens jointly with OSHA.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: And then a lot of times OSHA does rely on our investigative reports related specifically to fatalities as part of their enforcement actions.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: As well.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Commissioner and Deputy Commissioner.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks how DOB oversees small sites below the site safety manager threshold; Tigani says trained competent individuals are still required, same rules and enforcement apply, and proactive enforcement builds a hotspot database, while Shamash notes construction super requirements extend to all new buildings and major alterations and the new one-job-site limit takes effect at year's end.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks how DOB oversees safety at small sites

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So my last question, just to close, you know, coming back to the issue of small sites, how would you describe the ways in which DOB oversees safety at small sites that fall below the threshold for a site safety manager or coordinator?

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: So we still require competent individuals with training that includes being aware of both culture and best practice on safety to be on new construction on small sites.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: We still have the same rules and regulations apply and expectations apply, including the same enforcement actions.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Additionally, with the proactive enforcement work, we're able to get more data

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: and build a better database of where we think hotspots or dangerous activities happening, which can include small sites as we build up the proactive enforcement work.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: And then, of course, we always have our reactive work that's either feeding the proactive work or continuing to rely on our borough enforcement, real-time enforcement, and emergency response teams to make sure that workers are safe.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Beyond that, when we do construction safety outreach education, there's no division between small sites and big sites.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: We're trying to...

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: Disseminate and instill that education to everyone.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: I'll just add with regards to, and you mentioned this earlier, a major building, seven stories or 75 feet and above, require the site safety manager coordinator requirements.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: However, the construction super requirements are for a much larger pool of buildings, any new building.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: Any major alteration where you're renovating more than 50% of the floor area,

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: vertical or horizontal enlargements, full demolitions, all must have a registered construction super, and that is a registration that they have with the Department of Buildings.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: And lastly, we have new regulations on the number of job sites a construction super can oversee.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: At the end of this year, that will be one job site per construction super, and that is a change that originally started from...

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: 10 sites that you mentioned it's hard to get to six locations.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: So these folks supposedly were getting to 10.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: Over the years, we have reduced that from 10 to 5 to 3 and now to 1.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: So we will have one very dedicated individual that is responsible to oversee construction safety and ensure that the work on that site.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: Is happening according to plan.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: And that is a big step for the department.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: and for the city as a whole.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: And one, two, and three homes, contractors are licensed through the department's DCWP, Consumer Worker Protection.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: So there is additional layers of licensing oversight for that level.

utterances.text: Contractors on one to three family homes.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks how much work is done by unlicensed contractors, electricians, and plumbers and how often DOB finds such sites; Tigani notes DOB licenses about 28,000 licensees across roughly 31 license types, publishes special inspection investigation data online, and describes three registration buckets, with Shamash promising specific numbers later.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks how often DOB finds unlicensed work

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: We do report, so there are different divisions that handle different parts of it.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: So we license over 2,000 trades, I think about 31 different licensees, over 28,000 licensees.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: This is done in addition to the work that the state, the Department of Education at the state level has in...

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: On this oversight.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: We do publish our data on investigations that the Office of Special Inspections does for unlicensed plumbers or unlicensed electricians.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: That's on our website.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: And then for

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: There is in the general contractor license, there's a safety registration that must be obtained through the department.

utterances.speaker: Ahmed Tigani
utterances.text: And I don't know if we have all those numbers, but I think you guys will share what we have.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: I can get you the specific numbers.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: Later, but we have three basically registrations, one for GC 123s.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: So those are general contractors that work on 123 family homes.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: And then as the commissioner mentioned, we have what's known as a GC safety registration.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: And then we have a general contractor insurance tracking number that we use to track other folks.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: So we have three different buckets of where folks can...

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: Fall into.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: The safety registration bucket is typically the folks that are doing the larger buildings, new buildings, alterations,

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: major alterations, again 50% of the existing floor area, generally fall into that safety registration bucket.

utterances.speaker: Yegal Shamash
utterances.text: I'll get you the individual numbers in each one of those buckets.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Sanchez opens the hearing to public testimony, reminding attendees to observe decorum, that the witness table is reserved for testifiers, that no video or photography is allowed from the table, that speakers get two minutes, and that written testimony can be submitted to the Sergeant at Arms or by email within 72 hours.
chapters.title: Sanchez opens public testimony and sets ground rules

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: All right, I now open the hearing for public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I remind members of the public that this is a formal government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times, like now, okay.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant at Arms for inclusion in the hearing record.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant at Arms and wait to be recognized.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: When recognized, you will have two minutes to speak on today's hearing topic of the administration's approach to construction safety.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: If you have a written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant at Arms.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: You may also email written testimony to testimony at council.nyc.gov.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Within 72 hours of this hearing, audio and video recordings will not be accepted.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: The second panel consists of Samuel Aluto from the Building Trades Employment Association, Rochelle Thompson, and Alex Lay.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And whoever is here can begin as soon as they are ready.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Alex Lay?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Yeah, you can come up to the dais.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And as soon as folks are ready, you can begin testifying.

chapters.summary: Samuel Ludo, Director of Member Relations for the Building Trades Employers Association representing 1,200 union contractors, praises Local Law 196 but flags operational problems with SST card checks, urging the Council to allow employers to verify cards by ID in advance and to define site-control due diligence; he also raises PVC pipe code discussions and a coming construction superintendent shortage.
chapters.title: Samuel Ludo of Building Trades Employers Association on SST card verification

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samuel Ludo
utterances.text: Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samuel Ludo
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samuel Ludo
utterances.text: I'm Samuel Ludo, Director of Member Relations for the Building Trade Employers Association.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samuel Ludo
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Sanchez and Council Member Zhuang for being here and for holding this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samuel Ludo
utterances.text: Our 24 associations represent more than 1,200 union contractors, and we have long worked with the DOB on safety, and we value the council's strong work on keeping New Yorkers and construction workers safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samuel Ludo
utterances.text: I'd just like to focus on the SST card verification discussion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samuel Ludo
utterances.text: With local law 196,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samuel Ludo
utterances.text: Council made New York the first city in the nation to really streamline the safety training tracking for every construction worker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samuel Ludo
utterances.text: There's just a few operational problems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samuel Ludo
utterances.text: I just wanted to flag on the SST card program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samuel Ludo
utterances.text: The only way to accept, to check a card is to tap it with a phone while the worker stands there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samuel Ludo
utterances.text: And so contractors can't really check workers who are dispatched the night before.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samuel Ludo
utterances.text: It's very difficult to check the cards the day of because the daily checks don't work at scale.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samuel Ludo
utterances.text: And liability falls on subcontractors who often don't really control the gate of the actual construction site.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samuel Ludo
utterances.text: And so we urge the council to amend the law and work with the Department of Buildings to let employers check a card by its ID ahead of time and get back only if it's valid or if it's invalid.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samuel Ludo
utterances.text: And also to define the due diligence of who really controls the site and to be able to have a plan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samuel Ludo
utterances.text: On how to check cards at scale when you have tens or hundreds of people, you know, on a construction site, this can get very difficult.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samuel Ludo
utterances.text: I just also want to flag a few things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samuel Ludo
utterances.text: I know that the mayor's block by block report in there's a lot of discussion about PVC pipes, plastic pipes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samuel Ludo
utterances.text: We think that the codes committee is a great place to do, you know, have these discussions with with experts at.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samuel Ludo
utterances.text: And we think that there really needs to be a substantive discussion that and through the experts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samuel Ludo
utterances.text: We also are concerned about the construction superintendent shortage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samuel Ludo
utterances.text: that's coming up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samuel Ludo
utterances.text: And so there needs to be more routes and more ways to support the pipeline of future construction superintendents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samuel Ludo
utterances.text: And we'll submit more things into writing.

chapters.summary: Sanchez welcomes ideas on expanding the construction superintendent pipeline and, on the record, says she will not cut off public discussion of plastic pipes, asking people to stop calling her office to shut down a conversation she is not convening and that should proceed so the best policies emerge; Ludo clarifies his association did not organize those calls.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez

utterances.text: Really welcome your ideas on how to expand this construction superintendent pipeline.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'm not going to cut off conversation about any topic.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez

chapters.summary: Rochelle Thompson, a 41-year rent-stabilized tenant in Harlem, urges the Council to protect seniors from predatory landlords, calling for guaranteed legal representation, automatic lease and income recertification renewals, and authority for HPD to enter buildings and fix tampered mixing valves; Sanchez cuts her off when she turns to a judge's ruling as off topic.
chapters.title: Rochelle Thompson testifies on predatory landlords and building conditions

summary: The Committee on Housing and Buildings held an oversight hearing on the administration's approach to construction safety, chaired by Council Member Pierina Ana Sanchez, with DOB Commissioner Ahmed Tigani and First Deputy Commissioner Yegal Shamash testifying.

DOB presented declining injury and fatality data, SST training numbers, proactive inspection results under Local Law 79, the 57 East Burnside Avenue and 222 Broadway enforcement actions, and new technology and sidewalk shed reforms; members pressed on staffing, small-site oversight, after-hours work, and fraudulent credentials.

Council Members Zhuang, Joseph, and Wilson raised district-specific cases, and six members of the public testified on SST card verification, the 2501 86th Street demolition, tenant conditions, and an Article 11 tax exemption.
